The “pacing the frontier” open letter is very bad. Let’s go line by line to discuss why it is bad.

Before that, let’s talk about the surface features: “Pacing the frontier” is impactful rhetoric, because the call for “pacing” distinguishes the group from the Pause AI people who are both publicly laughable in accusing innocent people of violence while harboring violent people in their ranks and using incendiary rhetoric that can and does incite unstable people to violence. So they’ve done a good job carving out a prima facie responsible niche here.

“Frontier” asserts that they are on the vanguard, and it fits since these labs are called “frontier labs” colloquially, but the term of art is already out of date (it should; it is several years old). LLMs aren’t really the frontier anymore, and neolabs working on multimodal models are producing much more exciting and impressive technology than the increasingly stale offerings from OAI/Anthropic.

But asserting from the top they are at the frontier sets the tone and asserts authority: WE are at the cutting edge, so WE need to be listened to.

In this sense, the framing is reminiscent of those “Architects and Engineers for 9/11 Truth” signatories, many of whom lacked the relevant qualifications to analyze 9/11 data, but leveraged an equivocation on words such as “architect” and “engineer” to claim expertise. I actually have a (former) friend who did this—he is a middle manager at Amazon who claimed to have special expertise in engineering to justify his belief that 9/11 was an inside job. You can see why we’re no longer friends.

Let me be clear (Obama) before someone reads this in bad faith: I am not claiming the signatories are conspiracy theorists or that they are being bad faith, and many of the signatories are probably just misguided or trying to manipulate public discourse for their own best interest. This is not an intentional equivocation across all signatories, but it is a latent equivocation in the presentation of the argument that is not discouraged.

To make it even clearer (Obama as preschool teacher): they aren’t willfully deceiving readers, but they are perfectly fine to go along with a misunderstanding on the reader’s part if it suits their goal of winning hearts and minds to push for a pacing of AI research.

Note that this is being presented as direct quotations from workers in these firms—that presentation is important too, because direct quotations feel both more tangible and real to readers as well as less filtered—there is a sense here that we are bypassing the limitations and restrictions of the big evil firm and getting the uncensored direct facts on the ground.

This is of course not true—after all, Anthropic’s CEO and several Anthropic founders have signed the letter—but since it lacks the more prominent CEOs who actually talk like CEOs (Sam Altman most notably), readers will overlook that.

Sam Altman really, really, really damaged OpenAI and the industry by insisting the technology he was building would both cure cancer and steal everyone’s jobs. This is one of the unforeseen consequences that I foresaw.

But OpenAI doesn’t listen to weird uncs in Thailand, because image is important and rhetoric matters. That I happen to be correct and have been for years is beside the point.

The first statement that is signed by all employees on the webpage will be the focus for most.

“AI could help create a dramatically better future, but that outcome is not guaranteed.”

They begin with self-serving antithesis: there are two options being presented. These aren’t logically exclusive of other options which are not hinted at but remain possibilities; the rhetoric is careful not to make false statements while also encouraging you to ignore the many many other possible futures that the text does not address. And the presented options tell you to choose between a better future or a different unstated outcome.

Any horror movie fan knows that the bogeyman is scarier when he is not revealed. By not stating the alternatives to “a dramatically better future”, the letter leverages your own imagination to get you to worry about all kinds of horrific possibilities. And since you’ve watched enough TV and movies with enough post-apocalyptic outcomes, you’re now entertaining an apocalypse as a live possibility. So of course, we need stewards to ensure that apocalypse doesn’t happen.

Self-serving point the first.

“The world's leading AI companies believe they could be close to automating AI research.”

Note how this is vague. Do they mean fully automated no human-in-the-loop post-training? Because if that’s what they mean, wow—none of this has been presented in the academic literature or in the releases from either the old AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic or the newer labs like Thinking Machines. In fact, what we see is billions of dollars going into companies like Mercor because human experts are needed to post-train the LLMs. Thinking Machines just had an exec quit because of how taxing the job is on her, the human being doing the work.

And note how the hedging reflects this distance: “believe”, “could be”, “close”. There are really three hedges in this sentence, but the average reader won’t pay attention to this, so they get to both be logically coherent and rhetorically impactful by addressing the idiots (who will respond with kneejerk loss-aversion fear) and the professionals (who will acknowledge that the labs probably do indeed believe this, because the labs are full of morons and grifters, such as several who signed this letter).

“It is hard to predict exactly how much this will accelerate AI progress,”

If it is hard to predict, why are we here? Why a warning about something in principle difficult to predict?

“ but there is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.”

This assertion is a bold claim, and bold claims require bold proof. Where is this risk, how real is it, how tractable is it and where did the risk come from? Because in my lab’s research, we see nothing of the sort—we are actually seeing significant low competencies in LLMs that demonstrate just how dumb these tools are without the painstaking post-training that leverages thousands and thousands of working professionals earning $200/hr. or more to help OpenAI and Anthropic do their post-training.

So, this should be shown more than stated. It won’t be shown, because it isn’t true.

“To realize AI's potential, industry, government, and society at large may need the option to buy time to address emerging risks, develop security measures, and strengthen oversight.”

The self-serving nature here is clear: because of the asserted and unproven danger of AI’s potential, society as a whole needs time to address the same risks we have been told are an existential risk to us all for several years now. Note too the “we live in a society” rhetoric, where the letter is claiming to speak for industry, government, and society by presenting them as their focus.

But just because someone claims to speak for society at large does not mean that someone claims to speak for society at large. And even if they do, it doesn’t matter. Just because someone is speaking for society at large does not mean they know what is best for society or their argument is valid. The temperance movement claimed to be working for all society when they made alcohol illegal in America in the early 20th century, and (no matter how you feel about alcohol) that is widely regarded as one of the biggest mistakes in the history of American domestic policy.

“But each company—and country—is under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration. And today, the world lacks the technical and governance tools to deliberately pace frontier-wide progress.”

There is an implicit logical connection here between the fact of intense competitive pressure and the theoretical success of technical and governance tools to stop that competitive pressure. Technical and governance tools can INCREASE competitive pressure and they often do.

However, let’s assume there are tools that can cause that competitive pressure to subside. Who feels this pressure? I don’t. Do you?

I feel opportunity, new tools and toys and fronts for research. I see an opportunity to get academics in linguistics and literary studies REAL significant funding to work on text and make better text-producing tools to lower how much toil you and your children will endure to make a living.

I don’t feel any pressure, because the benefits of this acceleration and its intense competitive pressure come to me, the consumer.

Workers in competitive industries are constantly pushed to work harder unless they are able to capture the regulatory environment and convince the government to use technical and governance tools to make their lives easier.

“Building on work already underway to monitor frontier model releases: We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”

And there is the real ask: they want a handout from the government in the form of technical and governance tools to deliberately pace the frontier so that their lives and jobs are a little easier.

No. Compete in the market like the rest of us.

If you’re good, you’ll win. If not, well, at least you had fun and it’s all about the journey, not the destination.

Claude does not need to be used for everything.
It can remain the home base, the platform handling most day-to-day work, while specialized tools take over the jobs they perform better.

Gen AI vs AI Agents vs Agentic AI.

Most builders confuse these.
Here is the difference.

GEN AI :-
What it does: Generates content
Examples: ChatGPT writing text, Midjourney creating images, GitHub Copilot suggesting code
Input: Prompt
Output: Text, image, code
Limitation: One request, one response. No memory. No action.

AI AGENTS :- 
What it does: Perceives, decides, acts
Examples: Auto-GPT researching a topic, a bot that books flights, a coding assistant that debugs and fixes
Input: Goal
Output: Action + Result
Capabilities: Tool use, memory, iteration, self-correction
Limitation: Single agent. Limited scope.

AGENTIC AI :- 
What it does: Orchestrates multiple agents to solve complex problems
Examples: Research team (researcher + writer + fact-checker), software dev team (architect + coder + reviewer), business automation (sales + support + fulfillment)
Input: Complex objective
Output: Coordinated workflow with multiple agents collaborating
Capabilities: Multi-agent orchestration, consensus, delegation, conflict resolution
Limitation: Complexity, coordination overhead, cost

THE EVOLUTION
Gen AI: "Write me a blog post"
AI Agent: "Research this topic and write a blog post with sources"
Agentic AI: "Run my entire content operation: research, write, edit, fact-check, publish & promote"

WHAT TO BUILD IN 2026

If you are learning Gen AI:
Build structured outputs, RAG systems, prompt chains.

If you are learning AI Agents:
Build tool-using agents with memory, iteration limits, and error handling.

If you are learning Agentic AI:
Build multi-agent swarms with supervisor patterns, consensus logic & human approval gates.

THE TRUTH :-
Gen AI is a tool.
AI Agents are workers.
Agentic AI is an organization.

Most builders stop at Gen AI.

The top 1% are building Agentic systems.
